points: Hydrocarbons are non-polar, because C–H bonds have very low polarity (see “Electronegativity and bond type”), so the only forces between their molecules are London dispersion forces.
London dispersion forces get stronger as relative molecular mass increases, because there are more electrons and larger electron clouds, and as the area of contact between molecules increases.

The stronger the intermolecular forces, the more energy is needed to separate the molecules, so the higher the boiling point and the more likely the substance is a liquid or solid at room temperature.
The nature of the carbon–carbon bonds decides chemical reactivity: single bonds only give unreactive compounds, while a C=C double bond gives reactivity through addition reactions.
Boiling overcomes the forces between molecules; it does not break C–C or C–H bonds.

notes.h: Straight-chain alkanes: boiling point and state
notes.b: The data show how boiling point depends on carbon number in the straight-chain alkanes.
points: Boiling points: methane −162 °C, ethane −89 °C, propane −42 °C, butane −1 °C, pentane 36 °C and hexane 69 °C.
Boiling point rises with carbon number because each extra CH₂ increases the relative molecular mass and the number of electrons, and lengthens the molecule, so London dispersion forces get stronger.
The rise for each extra CH₂ gets smaller: the successive differences are 73, 47, 41, 37 and 33 °C, because each CH₂ is a smaller fraction of the molecule.
At room temperature, about 20 °C, methane to butane are gases, while pentane and hexane are liquids.
Larger alkanes up to about C16 are liquids, and beyond that they are waxy solids.

notes.h: Straight-chain alkanes: solubility, combustion and reactivity
points: All alkanes are insoluble in water, because they are non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water.
All alkanes dissolve in or mix with non-polar solvents such as cyclohexane, following the rule “like dissolves like”.
Liquid alkanes are less dense than water and float on it; hexane has a density of about 0.66 g cm⁻³.
All alkanes burn completely to CO₂ and H₂O, e.g. C₆H₁₄(l) + 9½O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 7H₂O(l); larger alkanes need more oxygen per mole and release more energy per mole.

Larger alkanes burn with a more luminous, smokier flame and are less volatile, so they are harder to ignite; the percentage of carbon rises from 75.0% in CH₄ to 83.7% in C₆H₁₄, making incomplete combustion, with soot and CO, more likely.
There is no difference in reactivity: all straight-chain alkanes are unreactive, reacting only by combustion or by substitution with halogens in ultraviolet light.

notes.h: Isomers of the same carbon number: boiling points
notes.b: Alkanes with the same carbon number but different structures are structural isomers: they have the same molecular formula and Mr, but a different arrangement of the chain.
points: Butane (−1 °C) and methylpropane (−12 °C) are the isomers of C₄H₁₀.
Pentane (36 °C), 2-methylbutane (28 °C) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (10 °C) are the isomers of C₅H₁₂.
Hexane (69 °C), 3-methylpentane (63 °C), 2-methylpentane (60 °C), 2,3-dimethylbutane (58 °C) and 2,2-dimethylbutane (50 °C) are the isomers of C₆H₁₄.
The more branched the molecule, the more compact, or closer to spherical, it is, so the area of contact between neighbouring molecules is smaller.
Smaller contact gives weaker London dispersion forces and a lower boiling point, since the Mr is the same for all the isomers; unbranched chains lie alongside each other with a large area of contact.

notes.h: Isomers of the same carbon number: state, chemistry and diagram
points: 2,2-dimethylpropane, with a boiling point of 10 °C, is a gas at room temperature, although pentane, with the same formula, is a liquid at room temperature because its boiling point is 36 °C.

Isomers show no significant difference in solubility, combustion or reactivity: all are non-polar and insoluble in water, burn to the same products with the same equation, e.g. C₅H₁₂ + 8O₂ → 5CO₂ + 6H₂O, and are equally unreactive.
Diagram: two pentane molecules lying side by side with a large area of contact, beside two 2,2-dimethylpropane molecules touching at only a small area.

notes.h: Straight-chain alkenes: boiling point and state
points: Boiling points: ethene −104 °C, propene −48 °C, but-1-ene −6 °C, pent-1-ene 30 °C and hex-1-ene 63 °C.
Boiling point rises with carbon number for the same reason as in alkanes: a larger Mr, more electrons and stronger London dispersion forces.
Ethene to butene are gases at room temperature, while pentene and hexene are liquids.

Each alkene boils a little lower than the alkane with the same number of carbons, e.g. ethene −104 °C against ethane −89 °C and hex-1-ene 63 °C against hexane 69 °C, because it has two fewer hydrogen atoms, so slightly fewer electrons and weaker London forces.

notes.h: Straight-chain alkenes: solubility, combustion and reactivity
points: All alkenes are insoluble in water and soluble in non-polar solvents, like alkanes.
All alkenes burn to CO₂ and H₂O, e.g. C₃H₆(g) + 4½O₂(g) → 3CO₂(g) + 3H₂O(l).
Every straight-chain alkene has the same percentage of carbon, 85.7%, since all have the formula CₙH₂ₙ; this is more than in the alkanes, so alkenes burn with smokier flames than alkanes.
All alkenes have one C=C bond, so they all undergo the same addition reactions, e.g. all decolourise bromine water, and they are much more reactive than alkanes.
Changing the chain length or the position of the double bond makes little difference to reactivity.

notes.b: Use the data tables to predict properties from the trends.
points: To predict a boiling point, use the trend in a table: the value lies between those of the neighbouring members, or of isomers with more and less branching.
Pent-1-ene, with a boiling point of 30 °C, is a liquid at 20 °C but would vaporise readily on a warm day.
2-Methylpentane boils below hexane, because both are C₆H₁₄ and the branched isomer has a smaller area of contact.
Hex-1-ene will decolourise bromine water and hexane will not, and both will float on water without dissolving.
A mixture of pentane and hexane can be separated by fractional distillation, because their boiling points differ, at 36 °C and 69 °C.

keyTerms.definition: Weak intermolecular forces, caused by temporary dipoles, that act between all molecules and increase with relative molecular mass and area of contact.
The attractions between neighbouring molecules, which are overcome, not broken bonds, when a substance boils.
Compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in a molecule, written Mr.
The part of a molecule's surface that touches its neighbours, which is larger for straight-chain molecules than for branched isomers.
The principle that substances dissolve in solvents of similar polarity, so non-polar hydrocarbons dissolve in non-polar solvents.
Evaporating readily, which is the property of a substance with a low boiling point.

questions.prompt: The boiling points of pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are 36 °C, 28 °C and 10 °C. All three have the formula C₅H₁₂. Explain the difference and state which is a gas at 20 °C.
questions.model: All three are structural isomers with the same Mr, so the difference comes from shape rather than mass. Pentane is unbranched, so its molecules lie alongside each other with a large area of contact; its London dispersion forces are the strongest, giving the highest boiling point of 36 °C. The more branched isomers are more compact, with a smaller area of contact, so their London dispersion forces are weaker and their boiling points are lower: 28 °C for 2-methylbutane and 10 °C for 2,2-dimethylpropane. At 20 °C, 2,2-dimethylpropane, with a boiling point of 10 °C, is a gas, while pentane and 2-methylbutane are liquids.

questions.prompt: Explain why the boiling points of the alkenes ethene to hex-1-ene increase, why hex-1-ene boils at a lower temperature than hexane, and whether you would expect any difference in their solubility in water.
questions.model: The boiling points rise from ethene, −104 °C, through propene, −48 °C, but-1-ene, −6 °C, and pent-1-ene, 30 °C, to hex-1-ene, 63 °C, because the relative molecular mass and the number of electrons increase, so London dispersion forces get stronger. Hex-1-ene boils at 63 °C, lower than hexane at 69 °C, because it has two fewer hydrogen atoms, so slightly fewer electrons and weaker London dispersion forces. There is no significant difference in solubility in water: all the alkenes are non-polar, cannot form hydrogen bonds with water, and are insoluble in it.

questions.prompt: Hexane and hex-1-ene are both colourless liquids. Predict and explain one way in which their chemical properties differ and one way in which their combustion differs.
questions.model: Chemical properties: hex-1-ene has a C=C double bond and undergoes addition reactions, so it decolourises bromine water; hexane has only single bonds, is unreactive, and does not decolourise bromine water. Combustion: both burn completely to CO₂ and H₂O, but hex-1-ene, with 85.7% carbon by mass, burns with a smokier flame than hexane, which has 83.7% carbon.
